title: Transactional Messaging
description: Use transactions to make message production and consumption atomic with your database operations.

data.text: Transactional messaging ensures that producing or consuming a message and updating a database happen atomically. Without transactions, a system can end up in an inconsistent state: the database might be updated but the message lost, or the message sent but the database unchanged. The outbox pattern and transactional consumers are the primary tools for solving this.

data.title: Common inconsistency scenarios
items: Application updates the database but crashes before publishing the message
Application publishes the message but the database write fails
Consumer processes the message and crashes before committing the database transaction
Consumer commits the database but crashes before acknowledging the message, causing redelivery

data.text: The outbox pattern solves the producer side of the problem. Instead of writing to the database and then publishing to the broker in two separate steps, the application writes both the business entity and the outgoing message to the same database transaction. A separate process polls the outbox table and publishes pending messages to the broker.

data.title: C# — Outbox pattern with EF Core
data.content: Save the business entity and the outbox message in a single DbContext transaction.

data.caption: Outbox pattern ensuring atomic database write and message production
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Client Request] --> B[Application Service]
    B --> C{Same DB Transaction?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Write Order + Outbox Message]
    D --> E[Transaction Commit]
    E --> F[Outbox Relay Process]
    F -->|Polls| G[Outbox Table]
    G -->|Publishes| H[Message Broker]
    H --> I[Downstream Consumer]
    C -->|No| X[Inconsistent State]
    style E fill:#e8f5e9
    style X fill:#ffebee

data.text: On the consumer side, a transactional consumer reads a message and commits the database update in the same transaction. If the database write fails, the consumer does not acknowledge the message, and the broker redelivers it. Kafka's transactional consumer API is the most widely used implementation of this pattern.

data.title: Node.js — Kafka transactional consumer
data.content: Use KafkaJS consumer in a transactional group to process and commit atomically.

data.text: The inbox pattern is the consumer-side counterpart to the outbox. Before processing a message, the consumer inserts it into an inbox table within a transaction. A scheduler then processes inbox entries exactly once, avoiding duplicates from redelivery. This is particularly useful when the consumer is a public API that cannot trust the broker's redelivery behavior.

data.title: Idempotency Still Required
data.text: Transactional messaging prevents most inconsistencies, but broker restarts, network partitions, and human error can still introduce edge cases. Keep idempotent consumers as a safety net.

terms.definition: Saving outgoing messages in the same database transaction as the business entity, then relayed to a broker by a background process.
A consumer that processes a message and commits the result in a single atomic transaction.
Saving incoming messages to an inbox table before processing, enabling exactly-once processing from the consumer side.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The outbox pattern atomically writes data and messages to the broker
Transactional consumers tie message acknowledgment to database commits
The inbox pattern protects consumers from duplicate redelivery
Transactions reduce but do not eliminate the need for idempotency
data.takeaway: Transactional messaging is the structural solution to consistency. Combine it with idempotency for a robust, production-ready message pipeline.
